planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil; keep evenly moist through the first two growing seasons since this selection was found along a wet roadside ditch and does not tolerate drought.

directions: Site 'Betty Cummins' in a partly shaded woodland edge or rain garden with acidic, humus-rich soil that stays evenly moist to wet, since it was originally found growing along a roadside seep in New Jersey. This selection of the native swamp azalea stands out for its deep pink, clove-spice-scented flowers in June and July, a notable departure from the more common white-flowered forms of the species, and its dark green summer foliage turns orange to maroon in fall. Mulch with pine bark to hold moisture and maintain acidity, and avoid letting the compact root zone dry out during its first two seasons.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; give this vigorous selection extra room since it grows larger and faster than the straight species.

directions: Discovered by Bill and Tom Dodd near the Escatawpa River in southwestern Alabama, this selection of the native Florida flame azalea grows noticeably more vigorously than typical seedlings, reaching upright heights well above most straight-species plants. Fragrant gold flowers with wide petals and light red tubes open from apricot-and-yellow buds in mid-spring before or as the leaves emerge, carrying the strong honeysuckle-like fragrance typical of the species. Plant in humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil at a partly shaded woodland edge, mulch to conserve moisture, and avoid heavy pruning since flower buds form on the previous year's wood. It tolerates heat and humidity better than most deciduous azaleas, making it a reliable choice for Gulf South and Piedmont gardens.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in part shade; this selected clone forms a denser, more compact plant than typical seedling-grown sweet azalea.

directions: Selected by native azalea breeder Clarence Towe, this clone of the native sweet azalea produces unusually large, pure white, intensely fragrant flowers in late June and July, later than most deciduous azaleas, while holding a noticeably denser and more compact habit than typical seedling plants. Site in consistently moist, humus-rich, acidic soil at a shaded streambank or woodland-edge planting, since the species naturally grows along cool mountain drainages. Mulch to conserve moisture, avoid summer drought stress, and prune only lightly right after flowering to shape the plant, since flower buds set on the current season's new growth after leaf-out.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in average to clay, well-drained soil in sun to partial shade; this Chicagoland Grows introduction was selected specifically for cold-hardiness and can be sited in more exposed northern locations than many arrowwood selections.

directions: Trademarked Northern Burgundy, this arrowwood viburnum selection was chosen by Synnestvedt Nursery and introduced through the Chicagoland Grows partnership of the Chicago Botanic Garden and Morton Arboretum for its rich burgundy-red fall foliage. Flat-topped clusters of white flowers with yellow anthers open in late spring, followed by blue-black drupes that birds strip quickly. Plant in average, clay, or rich well-drained soil in full sun to dappled shade; this is one of the toughest, most adaptable native viburnums, tolerating both drier upland sites and heavier clay soils once established, and works well as an unclipped hedge or naturalized screen at a woodland edge.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; the narrow columnar form makes this selection well suited to tight side yards and foundation plantings where the species' wider habit would not fit.

directions: Introduced by the former Cole Nurseries of Circleville, Ohio, 'Royal Guard' is a narrow, upright selection of the native rusty blackhaw viburnum, reaching up to 12 feet tall while staying only 6-8 feet wide, considerably narrower in spread than typical seedlings. Like the species, it bears flat clusters of white spring flowers followed by fruit that ripens from green through pink to blue and persists into winter, plus deep burgundy fall foliage. Plant in well-drained, average to dry, well-drained loam in full sun to part shade; it is highly drought-tolerant once established and, in warmer parts of its range, appreciates light afternoon shade.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox
